disease_info: Specific Phobia is characterized by a persistent, excessive fear of a clearly circumscribed object or situation (e.g., animals, heights, flying, injections) that is out of proportion to the actual threat. Exposure almost invariably triggers marked fear or anxiety and leads to avoidance or intense distress, causing clinically significant interference in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning when the feared stimulus is encountered or anticipated. The course is often chronic if untreated, though many individuals structure their lives to minimize contact with the phobic trigger, delaying recognition until role demands change (e.g., new job requirements, caregiving roles, or travel). It is distinguished from other anxiety disorders by its narrow focus on a specific object/situation, absence of pervasive worry or unexpected panic attacks, and relative absence of fears about social evaluation or multiple domains.

narrative.stressor: About seven months ago, Oliver was promoted into a role that required him to start delivering more in-person training sessions at corporate clients’ offices rather than just designing the materials from behind his computer. One assignment involved a two-day workshop at a company whose headquarters were on the 32nd floor of a glass-walled high-rise in Boston, with floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the city. He had always been a little uneasy with heights but had managed this on hikes by choosing safer-feeling trails; in this new work setting he couldn’t easily opt out, and the combination of glass elevators and exposed conference rooms made it hard for him to function as a calm facilitator. Over the next several months he began turning down higher-profile assignments, trying to push colleagues to take any trainings in tall buildings, and eventually his supervisor noticed the pattern and suggested an EAP referral, which led him to seek psychiatric care when he realized this fear was starting to limit both his career growth and his usual hiking and climbing hobbies.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I have this intense, over-the-top fear of being up high in tall buildings that doesn’t match what I know is the actual risk, and it’s starting to interfere with my work.”

narrative.stressor: Roughly seven months ago, on her way back from a weekend hike in the San Gabriel Mountains with her outdoor group, Erlyn was on a freeway when a truck in the next lane suddenly lost a ladder that smashed into the car two vehicles ahead of her, causing a multi-car collision. Although she was not physically injured and her car only had minor damage, the chaos of the scene—screeching brakes, shattered glass, and watching first responders extract a crying child from a crumpled SUV—left a deep impression. In the weeks that followed she increasingly relied on friends to drive to salsa class, took surface streets for even short distances, and turned down invitations to out-of-town hikes and cultural events that required freeway travel, which began to affect her social life and her ability to attend professional development workshops. When her principal gently confronted her about frequent late arrivals and her parents started questioning why she no longer drove to family gatherings, she recognized how much her life had narrowed and agreed to see a mental health professional through her insurance.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Anytime I have to get on the freeway, I go out of my way to avoid it or white-knuckle my way through the drive, and it’s gotten to the point where it’s really disrupting my routine.”

narrative.stressor: About seven months ago, Esteban’s clinic began a new outreach program that involved more home visits and community events, increasing his exposure to dogs in patients’ yards and at neighborhood gatherings. He had a long-standing discomfort around dogs from a childhood incident in Honduras when a neighbor’s dog chased and knocked him down, but he had mostly managed this by choosing routes and social situations where he rarely encountered them. With the new program, however, he found himself frequently needing to enter homes and backyards where dogs were present, leading him to reschedule visits, ask colleagues to cover certain houses, and avoid otherwise valuable community events in parks. When a respected elderly patient gently teased him about refusing a simple house call because of her small dog, he realized his fear was starting to compromise the care he wanted to provide and his reputation in the community, prompting him to seek psychiatric evaluation through a colleague’s referral.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Whenever I know I might run into a dog, the moment I get near one I’m suddenly overwhelmed with fear and tension, even if it’s just a small pet.”
